security_audit.summary: All seven static command findings are false positives caused by Markdown fences or inline code, with no Ruby or shell execution present. Semantic review identified unrestricted agent-controlled SQL execution and untrusted web research flowing into a downstream agent. Add database controls and indirect prompt injection defenses before publication.

remediation.issue: The database tool executes agent-supplied SQL without validation or authorization controls.
remediation.suggestion: Use parameterized read-only queries, allowlist operations and tables, apply a least-privilege database role, and require approval before any write.

remediation.issue: Retrieved web content becomes downstream agent context without an explicit trust boundary.
remediation.suggestion: Treat retrieved text as data, isolate it from instructions, detect instruction-like content, verify sources, and restrict downstream tools.

semantic_findings.title: Unrestricted Agent-Controlled SQL Execution
semantic_findings.description: The custom tool passes arbitrary SQL directly to db.execute and assigns the tool to an agent. Model-generated or injected SQL could expose, alter, or delete data.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The example directly connects an unrestricted SQL string to database execution and exposes that function as an agent tool. No validation, authorization, or read-only boundary is shown.

semantic_findings.title: Untrusted Web Content Reaches a Downstream Agent
semantic_findings.description: The research agent uses web tools, and its output becomes writing-task context without isolation or validation. Malicious pages could influence downstream instructions through indirect prompt injection.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The configuration explicitly combines web retrieval with downstream task context. The absence of a trust-boundary control is clear, although exploit impact depends on the deployed tools and prompts.

content.value_statement: Multi-agent projects often fail because roles, tasks, dependencies, and control flow are unclear. This skill provides practical CrewAI patterns for structured Python workflows.
actual_capabilities: Defines CrewAI agents with roles, goals, backstories, and assigned tools.
Structures tasks with expected outputs, dependencies, and shared context.
Recommends sequential or hierarchical orchestration based on workflow needs.
Configures planning, memory, and event-driven CrewAI Flows.
Shows class-based and decorator-based custom tool patterns.
limitations: Provides guidance and examples but does not run or test CrewAI projects.
Requires Python 3.10+, CrewAI, an LLM provider, and project-specific credentials.
Example code omits production controls such as authorization, input validation, and failure recovery.
Features and APIs may differ across CrewAI versions.

use_cases.title: Build a Research and Writing Crew
use_cases.description: Design agents, tasks, and context dependencies for a repeatable research-to-content workflow.

use_cases.title: Choose an Orchestration Process
use_cases.description: Compare sequential and hierarchical processes for a multi-agent workload with clear delegation needs.

use_cases.title: Plan a Stateful Agent Workflow
use_cases.description: Map events, routers, memory, and specialized crews into a controlled CrewAI Flow.

prompt_templates.title: Create a Basic Crew
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a minimal CrewAI team for [goal]. Define each agent, task, expected output, and execution order. Explain the choices.

prompt_templates.title: Structure YAML Configuration
prompt_templates.prompt: Convert this workflow into CrewAI agent and task configuration: [workflow]. Include roles, goals, dependencies, inputs, and expected outputs.
prompt_templates.scenario: Separating workflow configuration from Python orchestration

prompt_templates.title: Select the Process Model
prompt_templates.prompt: Assess this multi-agent workflow: [details]. Recommend sequential or hierarchical execution. Identify delegation boundaries, dependencies, and failure points.

prompt_templates.title: Design a Production Flow
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a CrewAI Flow for [system]. Include state, routing, memory, approval gates, tool permissions, error handling, observability, and test criteria.

output_examples.input: Design a crew that researches a market and produces an executive brief.
output: Research agent: gathers cited market evidence from approved sources.
Analyst agent: compares trends, competitors, and uncertainties.
Writer agent: produces the brief from reviewed research and analysis.
Process: sequential, with explicit expected outputs and a review gate.

output_examples.input: Should a support-triage crew use sequential or hierarchical execution?
output_examples.output: Use hierarchical execution when a manager must assign cases by specialty and resolve conflicts. Use sequential execution for a fixed classify, investigate, and respond pipeline.

output_examples.input: Review a CrewAI workflow that gives every agent every tool.
output: Primary risk: excessive tool access increases the effect of mistakes and prompt injection.
Recommendation: assign only task-specific tools and require approval for sensitive actions.
Validation: test denied operations, malformed inputs, timeouts, and partial failures.

best_practices: Give every agent one clear responsibility and measurable expected outputs.
Use least-privilege tools, validated inputs, and approval gates for sensitive actions.
Test task dependencies, routing, memory behavior, retries, and partial failures.
anti_patterns: Do not create many agents when a deterministic function or single model call is sufficient.
Do not pass untrusted retrieved content into agent instructions without isolation and validation.
Do not expose unrestricted database, filesystem, or network tools to autonomous agents.

faq.question: What does this skill help me build?
faq.answer: It helps design CrewAI agents, tasks, crews, tools, memory, planning, and event-driven flows.

faq.question: Does it install or run CrewAI?
faq.answer: No. It provides design and implementation guidance for a Python environment that you manage.

faq.question: When should I use a sequential process?
faq.answer: Use sequential execution when tasks follow a stable order and each output feeds the next task.

faq.question: When should I use a hierarchical process?
faq.answer: Use hierarchical execution when a manager must delegate dynamic work among specialized agents.

faq.question: Does it cover persistent workflows?
faq.answer: Yes. It describes memory configuration and CrewAI Flows with state, listeners, and routing.

faq.question: What production safeguards are still required?
faq.answer: Add authorization, input validation, least-privilege tools, approval gates, observability, error handling, and tests.
